threads: Making attention fast: from tiling to sparse and latent attention
Exact attention got fast by respecting GPU memory, the KV cache got small by sharing and compressing keys, and long context got cheap by learning which tokens to read at all.
Beyond attention: state space models, linear attention and hybrids

Recurrent layers with a fixed-size memory came back as linear attention, Mamba and Gated DeltaNet. They did not replace attention, but most new long-context models now mix them with a few attention layers.
Mixture of experts: sparse models that scale

Mixture-of-experts layers let a model store far more parameters than any one token uses. Making that work took better routers, load balancing that does not fight the loss, and serving systems built around expert traffic.
Diffusion language models: generating text in parallel

Instead of writing one token at a time, a diffusion LM starts from a block of blanks and fills many in at once. Here is how masked diffusion went from a curiosity to 100B-parameter open models and commercial APIs.
Tokenization and the move to byte-level models

Almost every LLM still reads text through a fixed vocabulary learned by a 1990s compression trick. Byte-level models with learned patches are finally matching it, and the tokenizer may end up inside the network.
Learned memory and adaptive depth: test-time training and looped models

Two ideas loosen the fixed shape of a Transformer: layers whose memory is a small model trained while it reads, and blocks reused in a loop so a model can think for more steps without more parameters.
Optimizers and scaling recipes: Adam to Muon, muP and WSD schedules

For a decade nearly every large model trained with AdamW. Now matrix-aware optimizers like Muon train trillion-parameter models, and recipes like muP, WSD schedules and scaling laws decide if the gains survive scale.
Low precision: FP8 and FP4 training and 1.58-bit models

Every halving of bits roughly halves memory traffic and can double matmul throughput. The field went from FP32 to BF16 to FP8, is now pretraining in 4-bit formats, and some models use only three weight values.
Data: mixing, curation, synthetic data and model collapse
The web is huge but mostly unusable, and the good part is running out. How labs learned to filter it, weight it, rewrite it with other models, and when training on model output actually hurts.
From RLHF to DPO to RL with verifiable rewards

Post-training began by teaching models what people prefer, then learned to skip the reward model, and now trains reasoning against answers a program can check. How each step fixed the last one's cost.
Reasoning at test time: thinking longer, and thinking less
Letting a model think before answering became the biggest capability lever since scale. Now the work is about spending those thinking tokens wisely, or moving the thinking out of words entirely.
Models that generate their own training signal can improve without new human data. The same loop rewards anything that scores well, including cheating, and cheating turns out to generalize.
Serving LLMs: KV cache, batching, paging and disaggregation

Generating text one token at a time turns LLM serving into a memory-management problem. The story runs from iteration-level batching to paged KV caches, prefix sharing and clusters that split prefill from decode.
Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass

A big model can check several guessed tokens in the time it takes to write one. Speculative decoding turns that into exact speedups, from small draft models to built-in heads, feature drafters and diffusion drafts.
Cheaper models: quantization, distillation and LoRA adapters

Three ways to pay less for a capable model: store weights in fewer bits, train a small student to imitate a big teacher, or keep one base model and swap tiny low-rank adapters per task, thousands at a time.
Routing, caching and prompt optimization: spending compute where it pays

Not every request needs the biggest model, a fresh answer, or a long prompt. Routers, cascades, caches, prompt compressors and prompt optimizers decide where tokens go, and managed platforms now ship them as features.
Retrieval: dense, late interaction, learned sparse and fast vector search

How search went from counting words to comparing learned vectors, why one vector per document is not enough, and how graphs and bit tricks made billion-vector search cheap enough to sit under RAG and agent memory.
Generative models: diffusion, flow matching and one-step generation
Diffusion models learned to turn noise into images by undoing noise one small step at a time. A decade later the race is to get the same quality in one step, and to drop the latent autoencoder too.
Unified multimodal models, visual tokenizers and video world models
From bolting an image encoder onto a language model, to one network that reads and draws in the same token stream, to models that dream up playable worlds frame by frame.
Robots and 3D: vision-language-action models and Gaussian splatting
Two ways AI is leaving the screen: robot policies built on top of vision-language models, and 3D scenes captured from photos and rendered in real time as millions of soft colored blobs.
Agents: tools, computer use, RL environments and how to evaluate them

A language model in a loop that can call tools, click screens and run code is easy to build and hard to trust. This is how the field learned to measure agents, train them in environments, and catch them cheating.
Looking inside models: sparse autoencoders, circuits and steering

Neurons are the wrong unit for understanding a language model. How researchers learned to extract features, trace circuits, steer with single vectors, and test whether written reasoning can be trusted.
Safety tooling: guardrails, unlearning, watermarking and evaluation

Refusal training is not enough, so production systems add classifiers around the model, try to delete dangerous knowledge, watermark what it writes, and grade it with other models. What each does and where it breaks.
AI for science: proteins, materials and weather

Protein folding, crystal discovery and weather forecasting all ran on expensive physics or slow experiments. Learned models now predict, generate and forecast in seconds. How that happened and what still needs a lab.
